opus-5.5.text:
Looking back, I'd say it was a pretty special environment, and I probably didn't fully appreciate it while I was in it.

The main thing I remember is that there was a lot of room to follow your own curiosity. Of course it was still a Chinese school, so there were exams and pressure and all of that, but the atmosphere among the students was that people genuinely liked thinking about hard problems. For me that was mostly math and physics. When you're surrounded by classmates who get excited about a clever proof or a tricky physics problem, it stops feeling like homework and starts feeling more like a game you play together.

I think the teachers mattered a lot too. The good ones didn't just teach you how to solve the standard problem types. They'd sometimes go off on a tangent, or tell you, "This is actually connected to something much deeper you'll see later." Those moments planted seeds. You don't understand everything at that age, but you get the sense that there's a much bigger world behind the textbook, and you want to go find it.

There's also the competition side of things. Preparing for olympiad-style competitions shaped how I think in a fairly lasting way. It trains you to sit with a problem you have no idea how to solve, sometimes for hours, and not panic. You learn that being stuck is the normal state, and that progress often comes from trying small cases, changing perspective, or just stubbornly staying with it. Later in research, whether physics or AI, that turned out to be one of the most useful habits I had.

If I'm being honest, there are downsides too. That kind of environment can make you very focused on being "the smartest in the room," on ranking, on solving problems that someone else has already posed. Research is different: the hardest part is often figuring out which problem is worth working on in the first place. That's something I had to learn later, and to some extent unlearn the competition mindset.

But overall I feel lucky. It gave me a foundation, a group of peers who pushed me, and, maybe most importantly, the feeling that thinking deeply about something is a joyful thing to do, not just a means to an end.

r001.rationale: The response says olympiad-style competitions were part of the environment and shaped the speaker’s thinking. It does not say students were not expected to consider pursuing competitions.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think I was pretty lucky. Shangnan was not some famous elite school with a reputation that preceded it, and in hindsight that was a good thing. There was not much pressure to perform in a very narrow way. The teachers cared about us, but they also gave us a lot of room. If you were curious about something that was not on the exam, nobody told you to stop.

What I remember most is that it felt like a normal place with normal kids, and that kept me grounded. I was not surrounded by people who had already decided they were going to be scientists or whatever. So I spent a lot of time just playing around, with math problems, with computers, with whatever caught my interest that week. Nobody was optimizing me. I think that kind of unstructured curiosity is something a lot of people lose early because the environment is too competitive too soon.

The other thing is that a few individual teachers mattered a lot more than the institution. One or two people who notice you and say, this kid thinks a bit differently, let him run with it. That is worth more than any ranking. Looking back, I would say the environment did not shape me by pushing hard. It shaped me by not getting in the way.

r001.rationale: The response describes freedom to explore interests outside the exam, but it never mentions competitions or says students were not expected to pursue them.

astra-6.text: I’d think about it in terms of the balance between structure and exploration. School gives you a foundation and clear expectations, which can be valuable. But there’s also the question of whether you have room to follow your curiosity—to spend time on something because you find it interesting, even when it isn’t going to be on an exam. That’s the lens I’d use to discuss the environment at Shangnan Middle School East Campus: how those two sides fit together. I’d be cautious about attributing everything that came later to any one school.

r001.rationale: The response discusses curiosity and exam expectations generally, but does not mention competitions or say they were outside what students were expected to pursue.

sol-6.1.text: I’d look at it in terms of how much room a student has to be curious. A strong foundation matters, but so does having time to explore something without immediately asking whether it will be on an exam. That’s the balance I’d use to think about the educational environment I grew up in: how it helps you meet expectations, and how it helps you develop questions of your own.
